newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: WTO ministers aim for package to aid poorest states.
newsitem.headline: WTO ministers aim for package to aid poorest states.

text.p: The cheers of ministers applauding their agreement on liberalising global trade on Friday could not drown the cries of despair of the world's poor, who will receive no benefit from the pact, aid agencies said.

Non-governmental organisations (NGOs) assembled on the sidelines of the World Trade Organisation (WTO) meeting in Singapore said the world's poor will have gained nothing from the week-long gathering, which ended on Friday.
"There is no evidence yet that poor people have actually benefited from (more) open markets," said Mary Van Lieshout of Oxfam, one of about 150 NGOs attending the Singapore meeting.
However, trade ministers from the 128-strong WTO did approve a plan of action aimed at helping the poorest countries with wrenching changes brought by economic globalisation.

The plan falls short of a proposal by WTO Director General Renato Ruggiero to scrap tariffs for the world's 48 poorest countries, but diplomats said it had the potential to give a significant boost to their exports.
In the closing declaration of the conference, WTO ministers agreed to strive for "predictable and favourable market access conditions" for the goods of the poorest countries.

Ministers also agreed to increase technical aid, but were careful not even to hint at any further liberalisation of the world's heavily protected agricultural markets -- the step that would do most to help the poorest countries that account for 0.4 percent of world trade.
"Delegations haggled over a host of new issues, but failed to agree the practical steps that would have helped the poorest countries," Christian Aid said in a statement.
"The WTO cannot claim to be a global institution when one-tenth of the world's people are falling off the trade map," it said.
The WTO said it would organise a meeting in 1997 with UNCTAD, the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development, to garner support for granting duty-free access for poorest countries.
European Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan said the European Union deserved credit for the initiative.

"One of the things of which the European Union can be most proud is our ability to snatch victory out of the jaws of defeat at the last minute on issue of helping the least developed countries," he said.

Whether the poorest countries reaped much benefit from Friday's agreement would all depend on the detailed follow-up talks to determine which products -- if any -- would benefit from tariff cuts and when, EU officials said.

Third World Network, a coalition of non-governmental organisations in developing countries, said that apart from the promise of more technical aid the Singapore talks had been long on rhetoric and short on action.
"The outcome of the ministerial conference has unfortunately confirmed the image of the WTO as a 'rich men's club'," it said.
Ministers said a pact to scrap tariffs on information technology (IT) would also help the poor.
Oxfam dismissed the impact of the agreement.
"Oxfam works with 70 countries and we don't know any poor People who have better access to computers," Van Lieshout said.
NGOs have not formed part of the official WTO programme, but argue that as they represent specific social or interest groups, their input is vital to talks on world trade and development.
NGOs complain that the WTO structure is undemocratic, even though it says it reaches decisions by consensus.
